results.summary: This design implements a binary clock that counts hours, minutes, and seconds using registers and displays the time on a multiplexed array of 12 LEDs. It supports an optional pulse-per-second input for accurate timekeeping and allows presetting the hours via input pins. The design requires external hardware: a matrix of 12 LEDs and optionally a real-time clock or GPS with PPS output. It is notable for its efficient use of only 7 outputs to control 12 LEDs through multiplexing.

The RV8U is an 8-bit processor core based on a reduced RISC-V instruction set architecture. It executes instructions from external memory, which must be interfaced through the 8 input and 8 output pins configured as a serial-deserializer (SERDES) link. The design is intended to be tested with external memory, but the documentation provides minimal details on the instruction set and testing procedure. Notable for being a compact RISC-V microcore, but the lack of comprehensive documentation limits understanding of its capabilities.

This project is a test harness for various auto-generated Verilog implementations of synchronous and asynchronous logic gates, including latches and an edge detector. The documentation is incomplete, stating that a larger description and testing instructions will follow, but it mentions five components to test. No external hardware is required. Due to the sparse documentation, it is unclear how the design is used or what specific results are expected.

This design implements an 8-bit floating-point multiplier using the E4M3 format, with a custom approximation of IEEE 754 that flushes denormals to zero and saturates overflows. It accepts two 8-bit operands serially through a 4-bit data bus and control signals, and outputs the 8-bit product continuously. The multiplier has been verified over all possible input pairs and includes round-to-nearest-even. It is notable for its compact size and complete verification, though it requires manual clocking and external control to load operands.

This design allows a user to tap a button twice to set a beat tempo, which then causes the eight outputs to chase in a barrel-shift pattern at that rate. When the mode pin is not asserted, the first output emits digital noise generated by an LFSR. It requires external hardware: a button for tapping, a switch for mode selection, LEDs on the outputs, and an audio amplifier for the noise output. Notable for its simple interactive beat detection and noise generation, implemented in Amaranth.

This design scrolls binary data (0s and 1s) from an input pin across an 8x8 SK9822 LED matrix display. It uses a simple font to represent the binary digits and outputs clock and data signals compatible with the SK9822 protocol. The design requires an external 8x8 SK9822 LED matrix and a 3.3V to 5V logic level shifter. It was tested using an iCEstick FPGA evaluation kit, but the documentation does not provide detailed testing steps.

Zinnia+ is a minimal 8-bit CPU based on the Harvard architecture, with internal data memory and external program memory accessed through the I/O pins. It uses a 6-bit instruction length and multiplexes the output between the program counter and the accumulator. The design requires external program memory and a bus demultiplexer for operation. It is notable for its extreme simplicity and educational value, with a testbench provided to compute prime numbers.

This design is a fully digital RGB LED driver that accepts WS2812 protocol data and controls three LEDs with 8-bit PWM per channel. It includes a dithering scheme for flicker-free dimming at low clock rates and can forward additional data to another driver. The design requires external LEDs connected to the outputs and a microcontroller to generate the slowed-down WS2812 input. It is notable for its robust clocked implementation and testbench.

This stack-based calculator operates on 4-bit values with an 8-entry deep stack and 64 bits of random access memory. It accepts 4-bit opcodes and operands through input pins and provides results via output pins, with modes to display the output register or stack contents on a 7-segment display. The design requires external hardware such as buttons, a DIP switch, and a 7-segment display for testing. It is notable for its stack architecture and detailed opcode set, though it lacks a program counter and must be sequenced externally.

This design implements two ring oscillators with the same number of stages to measure and compare their frequencies, and to test whether they can influence each other. It uses control signals to enable the rings and select which result to output. The design requires external hardware to sequence the reset, enable, trigger, and select signals. It is notable for being a process variation and coupling experiment, but the documentation is minimal and does not provide detailed measurement procedures.
